claim: Homeostasis in adult tissues relies on the replication dynamics of stem cells, their progenitors and the spatial balance between them.
source: Homeostasis in adult tissues relies on the replication dynamics of stem cells, their progenitors and the spatial balance between them.
evidence: This is a general statement about tissue homeostasis that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Renewal of the tissue is due to progenitor cells that have limited replication capacity.
source: Renewal of the tissue is due to progenitor cells that have limited replication capacity (Watt and Hogan, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Watt and Hogan, 2000.

claim: Two opposing limiting models of stem cell replication have been proposed: A 'Hierarchical' model and an 'Equipotent' model.
source: For example, two opposing limiting models of stem cell replication have been proposed: A 'Hierarchical' model where stem cells are rare slow-dividing cells with longevity similar to the hematopoietic stem cell paradigm (Orkin and Zon, 2008) and a 'Equipotent' model where stem-cells are abundant equipotent cells that divide frequently and their loss is dictated by neutral drift (Klein and Simons, 2011; Klein et al., 2010; Losick and Desplan, 2008; Lopez-Garcia et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing these two models.

claim: Some studies assume a long-range correlation between replication and cell removal.
source: Some studies assume a long-range correlation between replication and cell removal, that is, as a cell replicates, the removed cell can be tens and even hundreds of cells away (Lobo et al., 2016; Richardson et al., 2018; Park et al., 2019; Richardson et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Other studies suggest short-range correlations between replication and removal.
source: and other studies, in different experimental systems, suggest short-range correlations between replication and removal (Mesa et al., 2018; Miroshnikova et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in different experimental systems.

claim: The cornea acts as a lens that focuses light into the eye, and serves as a barrier that protects the eye against external hazards or injury.
source: The cornea acts as a lens that focuses light into the eye, and serves as a barrier that protects the eye against external hazards or injury.
evidence: This is established knowledge about corneal function.

claim: Maintaining corneal integrity and continuous regeneration is crucial for proper vision in vertebrates.
source: Thus, maintaining its integrity and its continuous regeneration is crucial for proper vision in vertebrates (Yazdanpanah et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The regeneration of the corneal epithelium in homeostasis is due to limbal epithelial stem cells (LESCs) residing at the limbus.
source: It is now predominantly accepted that the regeneration of the corneal epithelium, in homeostasis, is due to limbal epithelial stem cells (LESCs) residing at the circumference of the cornea, the limbus, which separates the cornea from the conjunctiva (Figure 1A; O'Callaghan and Daniels, 2011; Cotsarelis et al., 1989; Pellegrini et al., 1997; Lavker et al., 2004; Davanger and Evensen, 1971; Dziasko and Daniels, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: LESCs divide both symmetrically and asymmetrically to yield progenitor cells that have a limited replicative lifespan (RLS).
source: LESCs divide both symmetrically and asymmetrically to yield progenitor cells that have a limited replicative lifespan (RLS) (Lehrer et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lehrer et al., 1998.

claim: Progenitor cells proliferate from the limbus to the basal cornea where they can either proliferate or migrate to upper layers.
source: In turn, progenitor cells are proliferating from the limbus to the basal cornea where they can either proliferate or migrate to upper layers (Figure 1A; Lehrer et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The 'XYZ hypothesis' states that the proliferation of epithelial cells in the limbus and their migration to the cornea is balanced by cell loss.
source: The observation that in homeostasis the overall number of cells in the cornea does not fluctuate dramatically led to the 'XYZ hypothesis' that states that the proliferation of epithelial cells in the limbus and their migration to the cornea is balanced by cell loss (Thoft, 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thoft, 1983.

claim: Lineage-tracing experiments in living mice revealed a pattern of clonal stripes that propagate from the limbus toward the center of the cornea.
source: Lineage-tracing experiments in living mice revealed a pattern of clonal stripes that propagate from the limbus toward the center of the cornea (Figure 1B and Appendix 1 section I) (Amitai-Lange et al., 2015; Di Girolamo et al., 2015; Dorà et al., 2015; Nasser et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The underlying mechanism behind centripetal migration dynamics in the corneal epithelium homeostasis is not fully understood.
source: Yet, the underlying mechanism behind these dynamics is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The authors developed a mathematical model for the stochastic spatial dynamics that underlie the rejuvenation of corneal epithelium.
source: We developed a mathematical model for the stochastic spatial dynamics that underlie the rejuvenation of corneal epithelium.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the work performed in this study.

claim: The model takes into account different spatial correlations between cell replication and cell removal.
source: Our model takes into account different spatial correlations between cell replication and cell removal.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model developed in this study.

claim: The authors derive tradeoffs between replicative lifespan, spatial correlation length, and tissue rejuvenation dynamics.
source: We derive the tradeoffs between replicative lifespan, spatial correlation length, and tissue rejuvenation dynamics.
evidence: This describes results derived from the model in this study.

claim: The authors determine the conditions that allow homeostasis and are consistent with biological timescales, pattern formation, and mutants phenotypes.
source: We determine the conditions that allow homeostasis and are consistent with biological timescales, pattern formation, and mutants phenotypes.
evidence: This describes results from the study.

claim: The results can be extended to any cellular system in which spatial homeostasis is maintained through cell replication.
source: Our results can be extended to any cellular system in which spatial homeostasis is maintained through cell replication.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader applicability of the results.

claim: The authors developed a lattice-based mathematical model of the cornea's basal layer.
source: We developed a lattice-based mathematical model of the cornea's basal layer, to examine the potential underlying mechanisms and parameters that govern corneal homeostasis, centripetal migration and spatial order patterns as seen in the in vivo data (Appendix 1 sections I and II).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The model assumes two types of cells: stem cells (S) and progenitor cells (P) that have different doubling rates λs and λp, respectively.
source: We assume two types of cells: stem cells (S) and progenitor cells (P) that have different doubling rates λs and λp, respectively.
evidence: This describes an assumption of the model.

claim: S cells reside only in the limbus and can either divide symmetrically or asymmetrically to produce S and P cells.
source: S cells reside only in the limbus and can either divide symmetrically or asymmetrically to produce S and P cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes a feature of the model with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: In the 'Equipotent' model, P cells can reside only in the cornea.
source: In the case of the 'Equipotent' model, the P cells can reside only in the cornea
evidence: This describes a feature of one version of the model.

claim: In the 'Hierarchical' model, P cells can reside both in the limbus and the cornea.
source: while in the 'Hierarchical' model they can reside both in the limbus and the cornea, PL and PC, respectively.
evidence: This describes a feature of another version of the model.

claim: P cells can divide only symmetrically.
source: P cells can divide only symmetrically;
evidence: This describes an assumption of the model.

claim: P cells are limited in their maximal amount of horizontal replications - their replicative lifespan, RLS.
source: P cells are also limited in their maximal amount of horizontal replications - their replicative lifespan, RLS, a parameter which will play a major role in the forthcoming results (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes a key parameter of the model with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Dynamics are simulated using a stochastic 2D lattice Monte-Carlo approach.
source: Dynamics are simulated using a stochastic 2D lattice Monte-Carlo approach (Appendix 1 section II).
evidence: This describes the computational method used in the study.

claim: If the RLS is small, cells will exhaust their replicative capacity before reaching the center of the eye.
source: If the RLS is small then cells will exhaust their replicative capacity before reaching the center of the eye (Figure 2A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations shown in Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: If the RLS is one, in steady-state the renewed cell front will propagate to fill the local interaction neighborhood, m.
source: For example, if the RLS is one (i.e. a P cell can divide once and then becomes post-mitotic), in steady-state the renewed cell front will propagate to fill the local interaction neighborhood, m (Appendix 1 section V).
evidence: This is a result from the model with theoretical support in Appendix 1 section V.

claim: As RLS increases, cells can replicate further, and the renewed cell front at steady-state will be closer to the center.
source: As RLS increases, cells can replicate further, and the renewed cell front at steady-state will be closer to the center.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations.

claim: The steady-state location of the front is closer to the limbus than what is expected if it propagates an additional one cell toward the center for each replicative lifespan added.
source: The steady-state location of the front is closer to the limbus than what is expected if it propagates an additional one cell toward the center for each replicative lifespan added (the deterministic limit, Appendix 1 section V).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the model to a deterministic limit.

claim: Even if the RLS is equal to the radius of the tissue (R = 100), the front still does not reach the center.
source: For example, even if the RLS is equal to the radius of the tissue, R = 100 in our case, the front still does not reach the center (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: P cells lose their proliferative potential already in the periphery when RLS equals the tissue radius.
source: because P cells lose their proliferative potential already in the periphery.
evidence: This is an explanation for the previous observation based on the model.

claim: The expected minimal RLS which permits replacement of central corneal cells (RLSmin) is around 130 replications in the case there is no centripetal bias.
source: In the case there is no centripetal bias the expected minimal RLS, which permits replacement of central corneal cells, RLSmin, is around 130 replications (Figure 2B, Video 1).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 2B and Video 1.

claim: For RLSs that are above the critical value, the front can reach the center and a patched pattern is formed.
source: For RLSs that are above this critical value, the front can reach the center and a patched pattern is formed.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations.

claim: The emerging pattern in the coupled replication-removal case without bias is that of contiguous patches.
source: The emerging pattern, in this case, is that of patches (Figure 2B, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 2B and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The patched pattern resembles the in vivo pattern of mutants that lack certain genes thought to play a role in centripetal chemotaxis.
source: While this case does not provide clonal stripes, it does result in contiguous patches that resemble the in vivo pattern of mutants that lack certain genes that are thought to play a role in centripetal chemotaxis (Findlay et al., 2016; Kucerova et al., 2012; Mort et al., 2011; Douvaras et al., 2013) (Appendix 1 section III).
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and experimental observations supported by citations.

claim: Biased cell division orientation toward the center lowers RLSmin.
source: We hypothesized that biased cell division orientation toward the center (Figure 1D) would lower RLSmin and lead to a pattern that resembles the in vivo clonal stripes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: As the centripetal bias increases, a centripetal pattern emerges.
source: As the bias increases, a centripetal pattern emerges (Figure 3A, Video 2)
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 3A and Video 2.

claim: As the centripetal bias increases, the required minimal RLS for renewal goes down.
source: and the required minimal RLS for renewal goes down (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the case of ideal bias, the minimal theoretical value for RLSmin is approximately R/m.
source: In the case of ideal bias, the minimal replicative lifespan required for full renewal, where m is much smaller than R, is R/m (Appendix 1 section V).
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived in Appendix 1 section V.

claim: When m is five cells, the minimal RLS is about 20 replications in the case of ideal bias.
source: In our case, m is five cells which give a minimal RLS of about 20 replications (Fig, 3B, 3B-inlet).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the model parameters shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Previous literature attributed very limited replication capacity (RLS around 3–4) to short-lived P cells.
source: This result is interesting in light of previous literature that attributed very limited replication capacity (RLS around 3–4) to short-lived P cells (Lobo et al., 2016; Richardson et al., 2017; Lehrer et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a statement about previous literature supported by citations.

claim: The model imposes a minimal lifespan for progenitor cells that scales as the radius of the tissue divided by the radius of the local neighborhood in which cells interact.
source: It imposes a minimal lifespan for progenitor cells that scales as the radius of the tissue divided by the radius of the local neighborhood in which cells interact.
evidence: This is a conclusion derived from the model results.

claim: As the RLS increases, the renewal time decreases.
source: As the RLS increases, the renewal time decreases (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 3C.

claim: As the centripetal bias is larger, the renewal time is faster.
source: As the centripetal bias is larger the renewal time is faster.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: In the case of ideal bias, the limit on the renewal time is given by 2R/(m+1).
source: In the case of ideal bias, the limit on the renewal time dynamics can be captured as a one-step process with an average step size that depends on the interaction length, m (Appendix 1 section V). The limit on the renewal time is given by 2R/(m+1) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived in Appendix 1 section V and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When the radius is about 100 cells, the renewal time is approximately 35 replications, which amounts to approximately 100 days assuming a 3-day cell cycle.
source: In our case, where the radius is about 100 cells, it results in a renewal time of ~35 replications, which amount to ~100 days assuming a 3-day cell cycle (Lehrer et al., 1998; Sagga et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the model results and cited cell cycle times.

claim: Centripetal patterns can be formed even in the absence of centripetal bias, but this phenomenon is limited to a particular set of RLS and interaction lengths.
source: It was previously suggested that centripetal patterns can be formed even in the absence of centripetal bias (Lobo et al., 2016). We show here that this phenomenon is limited to a particular set of RLS and interaction lengths that are associated with slow corneal replenishment time and high post-mitotic rate.
evidence: This is a result from the model that qualifies a previous claim in the literature.

claim: For low RLS values in the uncoupled case without bias, a centripetal pattern is formed near the limbus edge, but the unmixing diminishes toward the center.
source: For low RLS values, a centripetal pattern is formed near the limbus edge. However, the unmixing is diminishing as the stripes are moving toward the center (Figure 4A and B, Video 3), similar to previous reports (Lobo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 4A and B and Video 3, consistent with previous reports.

claim: The emergence of a centripetal pattern in the uncoupled case without bias occurs only for small RLS values.
source: The emergence of a centripetal pattern occurs only for small RLS values.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: As the replicative lifespan is larger than a few replications in the uncoupled case without bias, the emergent unmixing becomes more limited to the edges of the tissue.
source: As the replicative lifespan is larger than a few replications, the emergent unmixing becomes more and more limited to the edges of the tissue.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: For RLS larger than 10 in the uncoupled case without bias, unmixed order formation is very limited.
source: For RLS that is larger than 10, unmixed order formation is very limited.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: Small RLS values in the uncoupled case without bias result in a high post-mitotic rate.
source: In contrast, small RLS values result in a high post-mitotic rate (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the low RLS regime of the uncoupled case without bias, the vast majority of the cornea is occupied by post-mitotic P cells.
source: Interestingly, while only very low RLS values allowed some organized stripe pattern, in these low RLS values, the vast majority of the cornea was occupied by post-mitotic P cells that continuously underwent centripetal movement as a consequence of divisions of limbal S and corneal peripheral P cells.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: The low RLS regime suggests no cell proliferation at the center of the cornea.
source: Thus, this regime suggests no cell proliferation at the center of the cornea.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: When the capacity of cells to replicate is low (RLS of only a few replications), the time required to get to the center is in the order of hundreds of replication times.
source: When the capacity of the cells to replicate is low, RLS of only a few replications, the time that is required to get to the center in units of replication times is in the order of hundreds (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is an inherent tradeoff between the renewal time and the centripetal order in the uncoupled case without bias.
source: Thus, there is an inherent tradeoff between the renewal time and the centripetal order.
evidence: This is a conclusion derived from the model results.

claim: In the uncoupled case with ideal bias and RLS of zero, the fastest renewal time is when there is a perfect bias toward the center.
source: For the maximal time: in case the RLS is zero, that is only the stem cells can replicate, the fastest renewal time is when there is a perfect bias toward the center.
evidence: This is a theoretical limit derived from the model.

claim: When the radius is 100 cells in the uncoupled case without bias and RLS of zero, the replenish time increases by a factor of approximately 10 to approximately 6000 corneal replication times.
source: In the case the radius is 100 cells, the replenish time increase by a factor of ~10 to ~6000 corneal replication times.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the theoretical model.

claim: In case of ideal bias and high RLS in the uncoupled case, the minimal time needed to renew the whole cornea is log2(R).
source: For the minimal time: In case of ideal bias and high RLS, in each corneal replication time the traced stripes double their length. Thus, the minimal time needed to renew the whole cornea is log2(R) which in our case is around 7.
evidence: This is a theoretical limit derived from the model.

claim: Adding centripetal bias to the uncoupled model increases the overall clonal unmixing.
source: As the bias increases, the overall clonal unmixing increases (Figure 5A and B, Video 4).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 5A and B and Video 4.

claim: The overall trend of mixing order in the central region is bias independent in the uncoupled case.
source: Yet, the overall trend of mixing order in the central region from which cells are removed is bias independent.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: RLS smaller than approximately 5 in the uncoupled case with bias provides high unmixing but results in slow renewal dynamics.
source: RLS smaller than ~5 provide high unmixing but results in slow renewal dynamics (Figure 5B), and still high post-mitotic rate (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figures 5B and 6B.

claim: A 1D model that considers only cell numbers as a function of time yields homeostasis for RLS values of 4–12 when taking physiological parameters.
source: The case of uncoupled replication-removal without bias can be approximated as a 1D model. In such a model, only cell numbers as a function of time are considered and there are no spatial limitations (Moraki et al., 2019). Taking physiological parameters, this model yields homeostasis for RLS values of 4–12, which are comparable to the RLS range that provides minimal renewal time without bias (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a comparison to a 1D model from the literature with results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: As the RLS is larger in the uncoupled case with bias, the time it takes a clone stripe to reach the center is increasing exponentially with RLS.
source: As the RLS is larger, the time it takes a clone stripe to reach the center is increasing exponentially with RLS.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: For large values of RLS in the uncoupled case with bias, as the bias is larger, the velocity of stripe progression is larger.
source: For large values of RLS, as the bias is larger, the velocity of stripe progression is larger.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: In the case of ideal bias and high replicative capacity in the uncoupled model, the minimal number of replications needed for a stripe to reach the center is given by log2(R).
source: The limit on stripe speed can be estimated in the case of ideal bias, that is the removed cells are from the center of the tissue, and high replicative capacity, the minimal number of replication needed for a stripe to reach the center is given by log2(R). (Appendix 1 section VI), where R is the radius of the tissue, which is around seven corneal replication times in the case R = 100.
evidence: This is a theoretical limit derived in Appendix 1 section VI.

claim: The renewal time of the entire tissue in the uncoupled case with bias exhibits a non-monotonic behavior with respect to RLS.
source: The renewal time of the entire tissue dynamics exhibits a non-monotonic behavior.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: For high RLS values in the uncoupled case with bias, the centripetal motion slows down the motion in the direction orthogonal to the centripetal direction and thus slows down the overall renewal dynamics.
source: For high RLS values, the centripetal motion slows down the motion in the direction which is orthogonal to the centripetal direction and thus slows down the overall renewal dynamics.
evidence: This is an explanation for the non-monotonic behavior based on the model.

claim: Under conditions of spatial coupling between cell replication and cell loss, external cue that imposes a bias of centripetal movement is required for the emergence of a centripetal pattern.
source: Under conditions of spatial coupling between cell replication and cell loss, external cue that imposes a bias of centripetal movement is required for the emergence of a centripetal pattern.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results.

claim: In the coupled model, there is a requirement for a minimal value of RLS that allows renewal, which depends on the replication bias and cannot be shorter than a lifespan of approximately 20 replications.
source: Another major constraint is a requirement for a minimal value of RLS that allows renewal. This value depends on the replication bias and cannot be shorter than a lifespan of ~20 replications.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results.

claim: Recent nucleotide analogue incorporation experiments suggest a progenitor cell cycle of 3–5 days.
source: Recent nucleotide analogue incorporation experiments suggest a progenitor cell cycle of 3–5 days (Sagga et al., 2018)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the literature.

claim: Complete renewal of the cornea occurs in mice in few months.
source: and complete renewal of the cornea occurs, in mice, in few months (Amitai-Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the literature.

claim: The normalized renewal time is in the order of 20–50 replication times.
source: Thus, the normalized renewal time is in the order of 20–50 replication times, setting 100 replication times as a conservative upper limit (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the case of uncoupled interactions without bias, centripetal clonal unmixing emerges mainly in the periphery and only for small RLS values below approximately 10.
source: In the case of uncoupled interactions without bias, centripetal unmixing formation is feasible under very specific constraints. Centripetal clonal unmixing emerges but mainly in the periphery of the tissue and only for small RLS values that are below ~10.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: For small RLS values in the uncoupled case without bias, the renewal dynamics and stripe propagation velocity are much slower than experimental observations.
source: However, for these RLS values, the renewal dynamics and stripe propagation velocity, of a few hundred corneal replications are much slower than experimental observations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and experimental observations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In some mutants that abolish centripetal bias, the resulting pattern is that of contiguous patches.
source: Another experimental observation is the fact that in some mutants that abolish centripetal bias, the resulting pattern is that of contiguous patches.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the literature.

claim: Models of uncoupled interaction cannot provide a pattern of contiguous patches while coupled models can.
source: Models of uncoupled interaction cannot provide such a pattern while coupled can.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing model results.

claim: In the case of uncoupled interactions without bias, the resulting pattern would be akin to 'salt and pepper' mixed pattern rather than patches.
source: In the case of uncoupled interactions without bias, the resulting pattern would be akin to 'salt and pepper' mixed pattern rather that of patches.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: Only the coupled model can explain contiguous patches in mutants with the constraint of RLS >20.
source: Thus, only the coupled model can explain contagious patches in mutants with the constraint of RLS >20.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing model results to experimental observations.

claim: Models that require a low replicative lifespan result in a complete post-mitosis of the central cornea.
source: Models that require a low replicative lifespan, such as uncoupled replication-removal without bias, result in a complete post-mitosis of the central cornea.
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A scenario of post-mitotic central cornea is not consistent with in vivo data.
source: A scenario of post-mitotic central cornea is not consistent with in vivo data; nucleotide analogue labeling experiments suggest that some (Richardson et al., 2017) or most of the cells in the central cornea are actively mitotic (Sagga et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and experimental observations from the literature.

claim: The interplay between the emergent pattern and the dependence on replicative lifespan and replication-removal interaction length is similar in the Hierarchical and Equipotent models.
source: The interplay between the emergent pattern and the dependence on replicative lifespan and replication-removal interaction length is similar to the case of uniform progenitor cells (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is a comparison between different model variants shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: In the Hierarchical model, both the number of clones in the limbus and in the cornea goes down until it is equal to the number of stem cells.
source: In the case of the Hierarchical model, both the number of clones in the limbus and in the cornea goes down in a similar fashion until it is equal to the number of stem cells. (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In the Hierarchical model, the dynamics of clone number are invariant to the interaction length and to the degree of centripetal bias.
source: These dynamics are invariant to the interaction length and to the degree of centripetal bias.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: In the Equipotent model, the dynamics of the number of clones in the limbus and in the cornea is different.
source: In the case of the Equipotent model, the dynamics of the number of clones in the limbus and in the cornea is different.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: In the Equipotent model, there is a monotonic decline in the number of clones in the limbus.
source: In the limbus, there is a monotonic decline in the number of clones.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: In the Equipotent model, the decline in limbal clone number is invariant to the interaction length due to the continuous competition in the limbus.
source: This decline is invariant to the interaction length due to the continuous competition in the limbus.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed result based on the model.

claim: In the Equipotent model, the dynamics of the limbal clone number and average limbal clone size do not follow the neutral drift dynamics during the entire time trajectory.
source: In the case of the Equipotent model, the dynamics of the limbal clone number and average limbal clone size are monotonically increasing and monotonically decreasing, respectively. Yet, they do not follow the neutral drift dynamics during the entire time trajectory (Appendix 1 section VIII, Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the model to neutral drift dynamics.

claim: In the Equipotent model, the limbal clone size distribution exhibits scale invariance.
source: However, the limbal clone size distribution does exhibit scale invariance (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: In the Equipotent model, the dynamics of the number of clones in the cornea has a bi-phasic shape that depends on the interaction length.
source: The dynamics of the number of clones in the cornea has a bi-phasic shape that does depend on the interaction length (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The normalized front propagation velocity is invariant to the stem cell dynamics and depends mainly on the interaction length and bias.
source: The normalized front propagation velocity is invariant to the stem cell dynamics (whether it is the Hierarchical or Equipotent model) and depends mainly on the interaction length and bias (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In the case there is a centripetal bias, the velocity of the front propagation accelerates as it moves away from the stem cell niche toward the center.
source: In the case there is a centripetal bias, the velocity of the front propagation is accelerating as they are moving away from the stem cell niche toward the center (Figure 7E, Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 7E and Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The front acceleration dynamics in the cornea is similar to the dynamics in the intestinal crypts, where cells that are higher on the crypt axis move faster.
source: This is similar to the dynamics in the intestinal crypts, where cells that are higher on the crypt axis move faster (Tóth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to dynamics in another tissue system from the literature.

claim: Spatial coupling of replication and removal dramatically influences the parameters that are needed for tissue renewal in physiological time scales.
source: Spatial coupling of replication and removal dramatically influences the parameters that are needed for tissue renewal in physiological time scales.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results.

claim: Recent studies suggested that replication and removal events in homeostasis happen in close proximity of a few cells.
source: Recent studies suggested that replication and removal events in homeostasis happen in close proximity of a few cells (Mesa et al., 2018; Miroshnikova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about recent literature supported by citations.

claim: Short-range interaction sets a minimal replicative lifespan.
source: The main consequence of this type of 'short-range' interaction is that they set a minimal replicative lifespan (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The limit for replicative lifespan is the ratio between the radius of the cornea and the radius of the local neighborhood in which replication and removal occur.
source: The limit for replicative lifespan is the ratio between the radius of the cornea and the radius of the local neighborhood in which replication and removal occur.
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived from the model.

claim: If cell replication and cell removal are spatially correlated, the replicative lifespan of progenitor cells should be much higher than traditional values which are an order of only a few replications.
source: This suggests that if cell replication and cell removal are indeed spatially correlated, the replicative lifespan of progenitor cells should be much higher than traditional values which are an order of only a few replications.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results.

claim: The interaction range m dictates RLSmin and tissue renewal time.
source: Another limit is imposed by the replication-removal interaction range, m. We showed that m dictates RLSmin (Appendix 1 section V), and tissue renewal time (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 3C and derived in Appendix 1 section V.

claim: As the interaction range is smaller, the minimal RLS needed for a complete renewal of the cornea is higher and scales as R/m.
source: As the interaction range is smaller, the minimal RLS needed for a complete renewal of the cornea is higher and scale as R/m.
evidence: This is a theoretical result from the model.

claim: For interaction range that is of the order of the cornea radius, the minimal RLS scales as log2(m).
source: For interaction range that is of the order of the cornea radius, the minimal RLS scale as log2(m) (Appendix 1 section V).
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived in Appendix 1 section V.

claim: Mechanical or chemical interactions that are local require a higher replication capacity of corneal cells.
source: That is, mechanical or chemical interactions that are local require a higher replication capacity of corneal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results.

claim: The relation between the interaction range and cornea renewal time is monotonic, t = 2R/(m+1).
source: The relation between the interaction range and cornea renewal time is monotonic, t = 2R/(m+1) (Appendix 1 section V).
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived in Appendix 1 section V.

claim: Increasing the tissue size requires increasing the replicative lifespan of progenitor cells or increasing the local replication-removal interaction length.
source: Another interesting consequence of these results is that increasing the tissue size (e.g. human and large mammals cornea and large organs) requires increasing the replicative lifespan of progenitor cells or increasing the local replication-removal interaction length.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results with speculation about larger tissues.

claim: Cancer in the cornea is relatively rare, and when it occurs, it is believed to originate from the conjunctiva or the limbus.
source: Cancer in the cornea is relatively rare, and when it occurs, it is believed to originate from the conjunctiva or the limbus (Basti and Macsai, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about cancer in the cornea supported by a citation.

claim: In the cornea, the number of cells is low compared to the number of cells in the skin or in the gut.
source: In the cornea, the number of cells is low compared to the number of cells in the skin or in the gut, for example (Milo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison supported by a citation.

claim: Symmetric divisions promote cell exchange and can flush out mutations, and therefore the Equipotent model is more resilient to mutations in the limbus.
source: In general, symmetric divisions promote cell exchange and can flush out mutations, and therefore the Equipotent model is more resilient to mutations in the limbus (Appendix 1 section IX).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis in Appendix 1 section IX.

claim: Centripetal bias decreases the depth of a lineage.
source: Centripetal bias decreases the depth of a linage, and the radius of the cornea imposes a limit on the median depth (Appendix 1 section IX, Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis in Appendix 1 section IX and Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: The typical lineage depth, together with the small number of cells in the cornea, suggests a low probability for an accumulation of a series of oncogenic mutations in comparison to other organs such as the skin or the gut.
source: The typical linage depth, together with the small number of cells in the cornea, suggest a low probability for an accumulation of a series of oncogenic mutations in comparison to other organs such as the skin or the gut.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results and comparison to other organs.

claim: A 1D model without spatial considerations can be approximated as a private case of the 2D work.
source: The case without any spatial consideration, such as bias and replication-removal correlations, can be approximated by a 1D model.
evidence: This is a statement about model approximations.

claim: A 1D model suggested that physiological homeostasis requires RLS in the range of 4–12 replications.
source: A model, which is a private case of our work, suggested that physiological homeostasis requires RLS in the range of 4–12 replications (Moraki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from a model in the literature.

claim: The 1D model estimate is consistent with the Equipotent uncoupled model in the absence of bias.
source: This estimate is consistent with our Equipotent uncoupled model in the absence of bias.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and a model from the literature.

claim: A 2D uncoupled replication-removal without bias was suggested in the context of the cornea with a replicative lifespan of fewer than about five replications.
source: A 2D uncoupled replication-removal without bias was suggested in the context of the cornea with a replicative lifespan of fewer than about five replications (Lobo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of a model from the literature.

claim: While rejuvenation of the entire cornea is possible for short replicative lifespan in the uncoupled case without bias, the rejuvenation time is much slower than physiological estimations.
source: Our results show that while rejuvenation of the entire cornea is possible for short replicative lifespan, the rejuvenation time without external bias is much slower than physiological estimations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 6A compared to physiological data.

claim: Self-organizing stripe formation in homeostasis without external cues is very limited and results in a rejuvenation time of hundreds of replications.
source: Thus, self-organizing stripe formation in homeostasis without external cues, while possible, is very limited and results in a rejuvenation time of hundreds of replications, that is, hundreds of days assuming corneal replication time of a few days.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results.

claim: The model that accounts for all features (tissue renewal, feasible dynamics, centripetal pattern, and contiguous patches) is that of coupled replication-removal dynamics with centripetal bias and a replicative lifespan that is at least approximately 20 replications.
source: The model that seems to account for all features is that of coupled replication-removal dynamics ('short-range interactions') with centripetal bias and a replicative lifespan that is at least ~20 replications.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing all model variants to experimental observations.

claim: One of the main predictions of the coupled model with bias is that cells should proliferate not only near the limbus but also closer to the center of the cornea.
source: One of the main predictions of such a model is that cells should proliferate not only near the limbus but also closer to the center of the cornea.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The results regarding the interplay between replication-removal interaction length and replicative lifespan do not depend on whether stem cell dynamics follow the 'Hierarchical' or 'Equipotent' model.
source: Our results regarding the interplay between replication-removal interaction length and replicative lifespan do not depend on whether stem cell dynamics and distribution follow the 'Hierarchical' or 'Equipotent' model (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a result from comparing model variants shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The number of clones over time on the limbus and cornea together could distinguish between the Hierarchical and Equipotent models.
source: As expected, our results show that the number of clones overtime on the limbus and cornea together could distinguish between the two.
evidence: This is a result from the model.

claim: The work highlights the crucial role of replicative lifespan of progenitor cells in shaping rejuvenation dynamics in homeostasis.
source: Our work highlights the crucial role of replicative lifespan of progenitor cells in shaping rejuvenation dynamics in homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: The conclusions regarding the interplay between replication-removal locality and replicative lifespan are relevant for any tissue in which conditions do not permit significant cell motility and spatial homeostasis is maintained through cell replication.
source: Our conclusions regarding the interplay between replication-removal locality and replicative lifespan are relevant for any tissue in which conditions do not permit significant cell motility and thus spatial homeostasis is maintained through cell replication.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader applicability of the results.
